chapters.name: Vehicle Inspection
chapters.summary: Why and when you inspect, what defects to look for in tires, wheels, brakes, steering, suspension, and exhaust, the seven-step pre-trip method, and checks during and after a trip.
keyPoints: Safety is the most important reason to inspect your vehicle.
Front tires need at least 4/32 inch of tread in every major groove. Other tires need at least 2/32 inch.
Steering wheel play of more than 10 degrees (about 2 inches at the rim of a 20-inch wheel) makes steering hard.
Carry spare fuses (unless you have circuit breakers), three red reflective triangles, and a charged fire extinguisher.

chapters.name: Basic Control, Shifting, and Backing
chapters.summary: Starting without rolling back, steering with both hands, smooth stopping, safe backing, double clutching, downshifting before hills and curves, and when to turn off a retarder.
keyPoints: Back slowly in the lowest reverse gear, and back toward the driver's side when you can.
Use a helper when backing, and agree on a signal for stop first.
Downshift before you start down a hill and before you enter a curve.
Turn off the retarder when the road is wet, icy, or snow covered.

chapters.name: Seeing and Communicating
chapters.summary: Looking 12 to 15 seconds ahead, using flat and convex mirrors, signaling early, flashing brake lights to warn drivers behind, and placing warning devices when you stop.
keyPoints: Look 12 to 15 seconds ahead: about one block in town and about a quarter mile on the highway.
Convex mirrors make things look smaller and farther away than they are.
Put out warning devices within 10 minutes of stopping on a road or shoulder.
On a two-way road: within 10 feet of the front or rear corner, plus 100 feet behind and 100 feet ahead.

chapters.name: Speed and Space Management
chapters.summary: Total stopping distance, how speed and weight change it, slippery roads and hydroplaning, curves, downgrades, following distance for large vehicles, and space to the sides, overhead, below, and for turns.
keyPoints: Total stopping distance = perception distance + reaction distance + braking distance.
Double your speed and the braking distance becomes about four times longer.
Following distance: one second for every 10 feet of vehicle length, plus one more second above 40 mph.
Empty trucks can need more distance to stop than loaded trucks because they have less traction.

chapters.name: Hazards, Distractions, and Fitness to Drive
chapters.summary: Spotting hazard clues in roads and road users, move-over laws, distracted and aggressive drivers, alcohol and other drugs, and staying alert and fit to drive.
keyPoints: A hazard is any road condition or road user that could become a danger.
It is illegal to drive a commercial vehicle with a blood alcohol concentration of 0.04% or more.
Only time sobers a person up. Coffee and fresh air do not.
If you are sleepy, the only safe cure is to get off the road and sleep.

chapters.name: Night, Fog, Winter, and Hot Weather
chapters.summary: Night vision and glare, headlight use, fog, winter checks and slippery roads, wet brakes, and tire, coolant, and radiator cap safety in very hot weather.
keyPoints: Dim your high beams within 500 feet of an oncoming vehicle or a vehicle you are following.
In fog, use low beams and fog lights, slow down before you enter it, and avoid passing.
Do not let air out of hot tires. Pressure goes up with heat and drops when the tire cools.
Never remove the radiator cap until the system has cooled.

chapters.name: Railroad Crossings and Mountain Driving
chapters.summary: Passive and active railroad crossings, how to cross safely, what to do if stuck on the tracks, choosing a safe downgrade speed and gear, brake fade, the downgrade braking method, and escape ramps.
keyPoints: A typical tractor-trailer needs at least 14 seconds to clear a single track and more than 15 seconds for a double track.
Do not shift gears while crossing railroad tracks.
Pick a low gear before you start down a grade, and use engine braking as your main way to control speed.
On a downgrade, brake until you are about 5 mph below your safe speed, then release.

chapters.name: Emergencies, Skids, Crashes, and Fires
chapters.summary: Steering to avoid a crash, leaving the road, controlled and stab braking, brake and tire failure, antilock brakes, skid causes and recovery, steps at a crash scene, and fighting vehicle fires.
keyPoints: You can usually turn to miss an obstacle faster than you can stop.
If a tire blows out, hold the wheel firmly and stay off the brake until the vehicle slows.
ABS keeps wheels from locking but does not always shorten stopping distance.
At a crash: protect the area, notify authorities, and care for the injured.

chapters.name: Cargo Safety
chapters.summary: The driver's cargo duties, when to re-check cargo, weight terms, weight balance and center of gravity, blocking, bracing, tiedowns, covering cargo, and loads that need special care.
keyPoints: Check cargo within the first 50 miles, then every 3 hours or 150 miles, and after every break.
Use at least one tiedown for each 10 feet of cargo, and never fewer than two.
Keep the load low: put the heaviest cargo under the lightest cargo.
You cannot inspect a sealed load, but you must still stay within weight limits.

chapters.name: Hazardous Materials Basics for All Drivers
chapters.summary: What hazardous materials are, why the rules exist, shipping papers, placards and identification numbers, and when you need the hazardous materials endorsement.
keyPoints: You need the hazardous materials endorsement to drive any vehicle that requires placards.
A placarded vehicle needs at least four identical placards: front, rear, and both sides.
Keep hazardous materials shipping papers in a door pouch, in clear view within reach, or on the driver's seat when you are out of the vehicle.
